When placed between enhancers or silencers and their target promoters, boundaries block regulatory interactions (Bell et al., 2001; Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Fly boundaries subdivide the chromosome into loops by physically pairing with each other.
claims.source: Studies dating back to the 1990s have suggested that fly boundaries subdivide the chromosome into loops by physically pairing with each other (Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental evidence from chromatin immunoprecipitation, chromosome conformation capture, MicroC, and direct imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Self-pairing interactions of fly boundaries are head-to-head.
claims.source: Self-pairing interactions are head-to-head. This seems to be a common feature of fly boundaries and has been observed for scs, scs', iA2, wari, Mcp, Fab-8, AB-I, homie, and nhomie (Fujioka et al., 2016; Kyrchanova et al., 2008a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The two boundaries bracketing the eve locus, homie and nhomie, pair with each other head-to-tail.
claims.source: The two boundaries bracketing the even-skipped (eve) locus, homie and nhomie, pair with each other head-to-tail, while boundaries in the Abdominal-B (Abd-B) region of the BX-C usually pair with their neighbors head-to-head.
claims.evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript (Fujioka et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Boundaries in the Abdominal-B region of the BX-C usually pair with their neighbors head-to-head.
claims.source: The two boundaries bracketing the even-skipped (eve) locus, homie and nhomie, pair with each other head-to-tail, while boundaries in the Abdominal-B (Abd-B) region of the BX-C usually pair with their neighbors head-to-head.
claims.evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The eve TAD is a 'volcano' triangle with a plume in wild-type MicroC experiments.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2, the eve TAD and the four Abd-B TADs have distinctive MicroC contact patterns. The eve TAD is a 'volcano' triangle with a plume.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The endpoints of the eve volcano triangle are delimited by nhomie on the left and homie on the right.
claims.source: The endpoints of the volcano triangle are delimited by nhomie on the left and homie on the right, and within the eve locus (the volcano), there are additional enhanced interactions.
claims.evidence: This is observed in MicroC data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Contacts between sequences in eve and the neighboring TAD on the left (TL) are much reduced.
claims.source: While the volcano triangle is generated by contacts between sequences within the eve stem-loop, contacts between sequences in eve and in the neighboring TAD on the left, TL (which contains multiple sub-TADs and six genes: CG15863, CG1418, Pal1, CG12133, eIF3j, and CG12134), are much reduced (L-ev in Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Contacts between sequences in the eve TAD and sequences in the large neighboring TAD on the right (TM) are suppressed.
claims.source: There is a similar suppression of contacts between sequences in the eve TAD and sequences in the large neighboring TAD on the right, TM (which contains TER94 and Pka-R2; ev-M in Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Physical contacts between sequences in TL and TM are enhanced compared to those between eve and TL or TM.
claims.source: On the other hand, as expected from the regulatory interactions observed for stem-loops in boundary bypass experiments (Kyrchanova et al., 2008a), physical contacts between sequences in TL and TM are enhanced compared to those between eve and TL (L-ev) or TM (ev-M).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 2A and is consistent with previous boundary bypass experiments.

claims.claim: The eve volcano triangle is topped by a plume generated by preferential interactions between TADs to either side of the eve stem-loop.
claims.source: Because of the preferential interactions between TADs to either side of the eve stem-loop, the eve volcano triangle is topped by a plume (L-M in Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The four Abd-B TADs (iab-5, iab-6, iab-7, and iab-8) have distinctive MicroC contact patterns that differ from the eve TAD.
claims.source: Like the eve boundaries, the TADs in the Abd-B region of BX-C region are connected to their neighbors by the boundaries at their base. As predicted from genetic studies on BX-C boundaries, each TAD corresponds to one of the four parasegment-specific regulatory domains. While the MicroC contact maps for the four Abd-B TADs resemble the contact patterns in the eve TAD, these Abd-B TADs differ from eve in that there are no plumes above their triangle peaks (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The Abd-B TADs are overlaid by a series of rectangular interlocking low-density contact domains, or clouds.
claims.source: Instead, the Abd-B TADs are overlaid by a series of rectangular interlocking low-density contact (LDC) domains, or clouds.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The iab-6 regulatory domain is flanked by clouds generated by crosslinking with its next-door neighbors iab-5 and iab-7.
claims.source: As illustrated in Figure 2B, the iab-6 regulatory domain is flanked by clouds generated by crosslinking with its next-door neighbors iab-5 (5–6) and iab-7 (6–7), followed by crosslinking with neighbors that are a TAD away from iab-6, iab-4 (4–6), and iab-8 (6–8).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the left endpoint of the eve TAD is no longer well-defined.
claims.source: While homie still defines the distal (relative to the centromere) end of the eve locus, the λ DNA replacement does not function as a TAD boundary, and the leftward endpoint of the eve TAD is no longer well-defined.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, one new endpoint for the eve locus maps to sequences between CG12134 and eIF3j.
claims.source: One new 'endpoint' for the eve locus maps to sequences between CG12134 and eIF3j (green arrowhead), which in wild type corresponds to the left boundary of the TL sub-TAD TL4.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, another endpoint maps to sequences between eIF3j and CG12133.
claims.source: The other endpoint maps to sequences between eIF3j and CG12133 (blue arrowhead), which in wild type define the left boundary of the TL sub-TAD TL3.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the eve TAD appears to flip back and forth between alternative endpoints.
claims.source: These interactions are not as stable as those between nhomie and homie as the density of interaction dots is lower. Furthermore, they appear to flip back and forth between alternative endpoints (as indicated by the green and blue double arrows in Figure 3F) based on the MicroC contact profile, which is consistent with a mixture of (at least) two conformations.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the MicroC contact profile in Figure 3D showing lower density of interactions and multiple potential endpoints.

claims.claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the homie boundary does not contact the λ DNA replacement.
claims.source: As shown in the virtual 4C at homie viewpoint in Figure 3B and E, the homie boundary interacts with the nhomie forward replacement, but does not contact the λ DNA replacement.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the virtual 4C data in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, eve stripe enhancers activate eIF3j expression in syncytial blastoderm embryos.
claims.source: As shown in the HCR-FISH experiment in Figure 4 and quantitated in Figure 5, we observed a series of eIF3j stripes over a dark background in pre-cellular blastoderm embryos.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR-FISH data in Figure 4 and quantified in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the highest levels of eIF3j expression correspond to eve stripes 1, 2, 3, and 7.
claims.source: While it is possible to detect all seven stripes in λ DNA blastoderm stage embryos, their levels of expression are not equal. The highest levels correspond to eve stripes 1, 2, 3, and 7, while eve stripes 4, 5, and 6 are expressed at much lower levels.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the HCR-FISH data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The stripe enhancers for eve stripes 1, 2, 3, and 7 are located between the eve promoter and nhomie.
claims.source: Since the stripe enhancers for 1, 2, 3, and 7 are located between the eve promoter and nhomie, they are closer to the eIF3j promoter than the enhancers for stripes 4, 5, and 6, which are located downstream of the eve transcription unit.
claims.evidence: This is based on the known genomic organization of the eve locus.

claims.claim: The nhomie deletion did not have any obvious impact on the level or pattern of eve expression in blastoderm stage embryos.
claims.source: While the nhomie deletion did not have any obvious impact on the level or pattern of eve expression in blastoderm stage embryos (see Figure 4), it seemed possible that eve activity was not entirely normal.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the HCR-FISH data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the frequency of larvae with two or more missing ventral denticle bands is increased nearly twofold compared to nhomie forward.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5B, the frequency of larvae with 'severe' defects (two or more missing ventral denticle bands) in nhomie forward is similar to that in a WT yw control. In contrast, in the λ DNA replacement, the frequency of larval cuticles with two or more missing denticle bands is increased nearly twofold.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The increase in severity of cuticle defects in the lambda DNA replacement is significant at the p<0.01 level.
claims.source: Taken together, the increase in severity of the cuticle defects is significant at the p<0.01 level (one-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the denticle band defect data.

claims.claim: Inverting the nhomie boundary converts the eve TAD from a stem-loop to a circle-loop.
claims.source: Since nhomie and homie pair with each other head-to-tail, the endogenous eve TAD is a stem-loop. This orientation dependence means that one can convert the eve TAD from a stem-loop to a circle-loop by inverting the nhomie boundary.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by MicroC data in Figure 6A showing the altered contact pattern after nhomie inversion.

claims.claim: The eve TAD is reconstituted by nhomie reverse.
claims.source: Figure 6A shows that the eve TAD is reconstituted by nhomie reverse (compare with Figure 3: see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In the nhomie reverse replacement, the plume topping the eve TAD is gone and is replaced by a much more sparsely populated LDC domain.
claims.source: In addition, consistent with our expectation, the plume topping the eve TAD is gone and is replaced by a much more sparsely populated LDC domain (purple double-arrow and above).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In the nhomie reverse replacement, eve forms an LDC interaction domain with TM on the right.
claims.source: On the right, eve forms an LDC interaction domain with TM (ev-M).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In the nhomie reverse replacement, eve interacts most strongly with sequences in TL4 on the left.
claims.source: On the left, eve interacts most strongly with sequences in TL4, and progressively less strongly with sequences in the sub-TADs TL3, TL2, and then TL1 (L-ev).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In the nhomie reverse replacement, the TL TAD is re-established.
claims.source: In addition to restoring the eve TAD, the TL TAD is re-established, indicating that the nhomie boundary is important in defining both endpoints of the TL TAD.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The nhomie boundary is important in defining both endpoints of the TL TAD.
claims.source: In addition to restoring the eve TAD, the TL TAD is re-established, indicating that the nhomie boundary is important in defining both endpoints of the TL TAD.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the restoration of the TL TAD in the nhomie reverse replacement.

claims.claim: The eve stripe enhancers in nhomie reverse are able to weakly activate expression of eIF3j and TER94.
claims.source: Figure 7 shows that the eve enhancers weakly activate both eIF3j and TER94.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR-FISH data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: In nhomie reverse, eIF3j and TER94 stripe expression is detected in only about half of the blastoderm stage embryos.
claims.source: In addition, eve-dependent eIF3j and TER94 stripes are detected in only about half of the blastoderm stage embryos (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In nhomie reverse, the frequency of embryos with two or more missing denticle bands is nearly twice that of nhomie forward.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5B, the fraction of nhomie reverse embryos with two or more missing denticle bands is nearly twice that in either yw or the nhomie forward replacement.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The increase in severity of cuticle defects in nhomie reverse is significant at the p<0.05 level.
claims.source: Taken together, the increase in severity of the cuticle defects is significant at the p<0.05 level (one-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the denticle band defect data.

claims.claim: The homie boundary pairs with itself head-to-head.
claims.source: To test this possibility, we took advantage of the fact that in addition to pairing with nhomie, the homie boundary pairs with itself (Fujioka et al., 2016). However, unlike nhomie:homie pairing, which is head-to-tail, homie:homie pairing is head-to-head.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Fujioka et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Inserting homie into the nhomie deletion in the forward orientation converts the eve TAD into a circle-loop.
claims.source: This means that it is possible to convert the eve TAD into a circle-loop by inserting homie into the nhomie deletion in the forward orientation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by MicroC data in Figure 6D showing the circle-loop topology.

claims.claim: The MicroC contact profile of homie forward is similar to that observed for nhomie reverse.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 6D (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the MicroC contact profile of homie forward is similar to that observed for nhomie reverse.
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing the MicroC data in Figure 6D and Figure 6A.

claims.claim: In homie forward, the plume topping the eve TAD is absent.
claims.source: The plume topping the eve TAD in wild type (Figure 2A) or in nhomie forward (Figure 3A) is absent.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: In homie forward, the eve TAD contacts TL and TM instead of being isolated from its neighbors.
claims.source: Likewise, instead of being isolated from its neighbors, the eve TAD contacts TL and TM.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: In homie forward, the eve enhancers weakly activate both eIF3j and TER94.
claims.source: Figure 7 shows that the eve enhancers weakly activate both eIF3j and TER94.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR-FISH data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: In homie forward, expression levels of eIF3j and TER94 at the blastoderm stage are low and are observed in only about half of the embryos.
claims.source: As was the case for nhomie reverse, expression levels at the blastoderm stage are low and are observed in only about half of the embryos (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In homie forward, the frequency of embryos with two or more missing denticle bands is twice that of nhomie forward.
claims.source: In addition, the functioning of the eve gene when it is in the circle-loop configuration is not as efficient, and the frequency of homie forward embryos with two or more missing denticle bands is twice that of nhomie forward (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The increase in severity of cuticle defects in homie forward is significant at the p<0.05 level.
claims.source: Taken together, the increase in severity of the cuticle defects is significant at the p<0.05 level (one-tailed t-test).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the denticle band defect data.

claims.claim: PREs were first discovered because they induce pairing-sensitive silencing of reporter genes.
claims.source: PREs were first discovered because they induce pairing-sensitive silencing of reporter genes (Americo et al., 2002; Kassis et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The ability of PREs to physically pair with each other may be their most important function.
claims.source: More recent studies have shown that the ability of these elements to physically pair with each other may be their most important function (Batut et al., 2022; Levo et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: Boundary elements are responsible for defining the endpoints of TADs.
claims.source: In contrast, boundary elements are responsible for defining the endpoints of these looped domains (Arzate-Mejía et al., 2020; Batut et al., 2022; Bing et al., 2024; Chetverina et al., 2017; Ibragimov et al., 2023; Stadler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Fab-7 is unusual in that it appears to be able to pair in both orientations.
claims.source: Of the endogenous (non-gypsy) boundaries whose functional properties have been studied in detail, only one, Fab-7, appears to be able to pair in both orientations.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous studies of Fab-7 boundary properties.

claims.claim: Fab-7 boundary activity depends upon factors that have been implicated in the functioning of PREs.
claims.source: However, Fab-7 may be unusual in that its boundary activity depends upon factors that have been implicated in the functioning of PREs (Kyrchanova et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kyrchanova et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Self-pairing interactions in trans may be largely responsible for the pairing of homologous chromosomes in precise register.
claims.source: This make sense, as the available evidence suggests that self-pairing interactions in trans may be largely responsible for the pairing of homologous chromosomes in precise register (Erokhin et al., 2021; Fujioka et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Head-to-tail self-pairing would uncouple the loops on the two homologs and sister chromatids.
claims.source: In this case, head-to-tail self-pairing would uncouple the loops on the two homologs (and sister chromatids).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the topology of head-to-tail pairing.

claims.claim: Volcano triangles with plumes are rare in the non-repetitive regions of the fly genome (~30).
claims.source: A survey of the MicroC contact patterns elsewhere in the non-repetitive regions of the fly genome indicates that volcanoes with plumes are rare (~30).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of MicroC data across the fly genome.

claims.claim: There are two volcano triangles with plumes in the Antennapedia complex that encompass the deformed and fushi-tarazu genes.
claims.source: For example, there are two volcano triangles with plumes in the Antennapedia complex, and they encompass the deformed and fushi-tarazu genes (Levo et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Levo et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Most of the euchromatic regions of the fly genome are assembled into TADs whose MicroC profiles resemble that observed for eve circle-loops and the Abd-B region of BX-C.
claims.source: However, since most of the 'euchromatic' regions of the fly genome are assembled into TADs whose MicroC profiles resemble that observed for eve circle-loops and the Abd-B region of BX-C, it is possible that much of the fly genome is assembled into circle-loops, not stem-loops.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of MicroC data across the fly genome.

claims.claim: If a significant fraction of TADs genome-wide are circle-loops, this would effectively exclude cohesin-based loop extrusion as a general mechanism for TAD formation in flies.
claims.source: If, as seems likely, a significant fraction of the TADs genome-wide are circle-loops, this would effectively exclude cohesin-based loop extrusion as a general mechanism for TAD formation in flies.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the incompatibility of circle-loops with the loop extrusion model.

claims.claim: Stem-loops in flies are formed by orientation-dependent boundary:boundary pairing.
claims.source: In addition, though stem-loops could be generated by a cohesin-dependent mechanism, it is unlikely that this mechanism is operational in flies, as we have shown here and in Bing et al., 2024 that stem-loops in flies are formed by orientation-dependent boundary:boundary pairing.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in this manuscript and cited work.

claims.claim: In the most common version of the loop extrusion model, the mammalian genome is assembled into an alternating pattern of stem-loops and unanchored loops.
claims.source: In the most common version of the loop extrusion model, the mammalian genome is assembled into an alternating pattern of stem-loops and unanchored loops (Davidson and Peters, 2021; Higashi and Uhlmann, 2022; Perea-Resa et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing the loop extrusion model.

claims.claim: The alternating pattern of high-density TAD triangles separated by regions of low-density contacts predicted by the loop extrusion model is not observed in published mammalian MicroC data sets.
claims.source: However, this crosslinking pattern is not observed in published MicroC data sets (Hsieh et al., 2020; Krietenstein et al., 2020). Instead of an alternating pattern of high-density TAD triangles separated by regions of low-density contacts, the TAD triangles are generally linked to both neighbors, just as in flies.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of published mammalian MicroC data.

claims.claim: There are few stem-loop volcano TADs topped by plumes in mammalian genomes.
claims.source: Moreover, also like in Drosophila, there are few stem-loop volcano TADs topped by plumes.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of mammalian MicroC data.

claims.claim: The crosslinking pattern between neighboring TADs in mammals appears similar to that observed for circle-loops in flies.
claims.source: Instead, the crosslinking pattern between neighboring TADs appears similar to that observed for circle-loops in flies.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of mammalian and fly MicroC data.

claims.claim: There are no obvious volcanoes with plumes in the high-resolution RCMC studies of Goel et al., 2023.
claims.source: However, there are no obvious volcanoes with plumes in the much higher resolution RCMC studies of Goel et al., 2023.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the RCMC data from Goel et al., 2023.

claims.claim: The MicroC profiles in the RCMC studies most closely resemble those seen in the Abd-B region of BX-C.
claims.source: Instead, the MicroC profiles most closely resemble those seen in the Abd-B region of BX-C (c.f. the Ppm1g locus in Figure 4 of Goel et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of RCMC data with fly MicroC data.

claims.claim: Compromising cohesin activity has minimal impact on the TADs in the Ppm1g region of the mouse genome.
claims.source: Moreover, compromising cohesin activity has minimal impact on the TADs in this region of the mouse genome, as evidenced from the MicroC pattern before and after knockdown.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of cohesin knockdown experiments in Goel et al., 2023.

claims.claim: In the A/B compartment model, the chromatin state of each DNA segment determines whether it will assemble into a discrete domain.
claims.source: According to this newer version of the compartment model, the chromatin state of each DNA segment determines not only whether it will assemble into a discrete domain, but also how the resulting domain interacts with next-door neighbors, next-next-door neighbors, etc.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the A/B compartment model.

claims.claim: The sequences included in the eve TAD and its patterns of interaction with neighboring TADs are essentially the same in NC14 embryos as they are in 12–16 hr embryos.
claims.source: To begin with, the sequences included in the eve TAD and its patterns of interaction with neighboring TADs are essentially the same in NC14 embryos as they are in 12–16 hr embryos.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of MicroC data from different developmental stages.

claims.claim: In NC14 embryos, eve is transcriptionally poised, probably in most or all nuclei.
claims.source: In the former case, eve is transcriptionally poised (Chen et al., 2013), probably in most or all nuclei, while in the latter case, the entire eve TAD is silenced by a PcG-dependent mechanism in all but a few nuclei (Nègre et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: In 12–16 hr embryos, the entire eve TAD is silenced by a PcG-dependent mechanism in all but a few nuclei.
claims.source: In the former case, eve is transcriptionally poised (Chen et al., 2013), probably in most or all nuclei, while in the latter case, the entire eve TAD is silenced by a PcG-dependent mechanism in all but a few nuclei (Nègre et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Nègre et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The transition from potentially active to silenced does not impact the eve TAD or how it interacts with neighboring TADs.
claims.source: However, this transition from potentially active to silenced does not impact the eve TAD, nor does it alter how the eve TAD interacts with the neighboring TADs that are (mostly) transcriptionally active at both stages of development.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of MicroC data from different developmental stages showing similar TAD structure and interactions.

claims.claim: In the CG3294 meta-loop, a TAD boundary located at ~2.0 Mb on chromosome 2L pairs head-to-head with a TAD boundary located ~2.8 Mb away.
claims.source: Shown in Figure 8A is a 2.8 Mb meta-loop on chromosome 2L generated by the pairing of two TAD boundaries, labeled blue and purple (block arrows).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: The pairing of the blue and purple TAD boundaries in the CG3294 meta-loop brings sequences in the TADs flanking the two boundaries into contact.
claims.source: The pairing of the blue and purple TAD boundaries brings sequences in the TADs flanking the two boundaries into contact, and this generates two rectangular boxes of interaction indicated by the arrows (see also blue double arrows in the diagram on the right).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: The pattern of interaction in the CG3294 meta-loop (upstream-to-upstream and downstream-to-downstream) indicates that the blue and purple TAD boundaries pair with each other head-to-head.
claims.source: As shown in the diagram, this pattern of interaction (upstream-to-upstream and downstream-to-downstream) indicates that the blue and purple TAD boundaries pair with each other head-to-head, and this orientation generates a large loop with a circle-loop topology.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: The 2.2 Mb meta-loop on chromosome 3L is generated by four TAD boundaries.
claims.source: The 2.2 Mb meta-loop on chromosome 3L in Figure 8B is more complicated in that it is generated by four TAD boundaries (indicated by blue, brown, green, and purple arrows).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: In the bin/Mp meta-loop, the brown and green boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail.
claims.source: As indicated in the accompanying diagram, the brown and green boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail as do the blue and purple boundaries.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: In the bin/Mp meta-loop, the blue and purple boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail.
claims.source: As indicated in the accompanying diagram, the brown and green boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail as do the blue and purple boundaries.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Pairing of the brown and green boundaries generates a large ~2.2 Mb stem-loop.
claims.source: Pairing of the brown and green boundaries generates a large ~2.2 Mb stem-loop that brings sequences in the TAD downstream of the brown boundary, which contains the Dhc64C and CG1808 genes, into contact with sequences in the TAD upstream of the green boundary, which contains the CG3238 and bin (binou) genes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Pairing of the blue and purple boundaries generates a small stem-loop bubble that links sequences in the CG7509 TAD to the TAD containing the Mp distal promoter.
claims.source: Pairing of the blue and purple boundaries generates a small stem-loop bubble that links sequences in the CG7509 TAD to the TAD containing the Mp distal promoter (blue arrowhead).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8B.

results.result: TADs in Drosophila are formed by orientation-dependent boundary pairing, where head-to-tail pairing generates stem-loops and head-to-head pairing generates circle-loops. The eve TAD is specifically formed by head-to-tail pairing of nhomie and homie boundaries.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the foundational knowledge about TAD formation in flies and are well-supported by extensive prior literature (C1-C4, C7) and are consistent with the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript (C5-C6). The orientation-dependent pairing mechanism is central to the study's design and is validated by the experimental manipulations.

results.result: The wild-type eve TAD exhibits a stem-loop topology characterized by a 'volcano' triangle with plume in MicroC experiments, with the eve locus physically isolated from neighboring TADs TL and TM, while TL and TM show enhanced contacts with each other.
results.evaluation: The MicroC data in Figures 2A and 3A clearly demonstrate the volcano triangle topology with plume (C9, C24, C29), reduced contacts between eve and neighbors (C10, C26, C27), and enhanced TL-TM contacts (C28). The nhomie forward replacement successfully restores wild-type characteristics (C8), providing strong validation of the stem-loop topology's physical properties.

results.result: Deletion of the nhomie boundary (λ DNA replacement) disrupts TAD structure, resulting in ill-defined TAD endpoints and ectopic activation of the neighboring eIF3j gene by eve enhancers, with increased developmental defects.
results.evaluation: The λ DNA replacement demonstrates loss of boundary function through multiple lines of evidence: MicroC shows ill-defined TAD endpoints (C12, C33-C36), virtual 4C confirms loss of homie-nhomie interaction (C37), HCR-FISH demonstrates ectopic eIF3j activation (C13, C38-C39), and cuticle analysis reveals significant developmental defects (C42-C43, p<0.01). The preferential activation of stripes 1,2,3,7 over 4,5,6 (C39) is consistent with enhancer proximity (C40).

results.result: Inverting the nhomie boundary (nhomie reverse) converts the eve TAD from a stem-loop to a circle-loop topology, reconstituting the TAD but changing its interaction pattern from isolation to enhanced contacts with neighboring TADs.
results.evaluation: The nhomie reverse replacement demonstrates successful topology conversion through MicroC analysis (C45, Figure 6A). The characteristic features of circle-loop topology are clearly observed: loss of the plume and replacement with LDC domains (C16, C46), enhanced eve-TL and eve-TM interactions (C15, C47-C48), and restoration of the TL TAD (C49-C50). This provides strong evidence that boundary orientation determines loop topology.

results.result: The circle-loop topology in nhomie reverse results in weak ectopic activation of neighboring genes eIF3j and TER94 by eve enhancers and partial disruption of eve function, with significantly increased developmental defects (p<0.05).
results.evaluation: HCR-FISH data (Figure 7, C51) demonstrates weak activation of both eIF3j and TER94, detected in approximately half of embryos (C52, Figure 5A). The cuticle defect analysis shows nearly twice the frequency of severe defects compared to nhomie forward (C53), with statistical significance at p<0.05 (C54). This regulatory disruption is consistent with the loss of physical isolation observed in MicroC experiments.

results.result: Replacing nhomie with homie in forward orientation (homie forward) also generates a circle-loop through head-to-head homie:homie pairing, producing MicroC and regulatory phenotypes similar to nhomie reverse.
results.evaluation: The homie forward replacement provides independent validation of circle-loop properties. The MicroC profile closely resembles nhomie reverse (C57, Figure 6D), showing loss of plume (C58) and enhanced neighbor contacts (C59). The regulatory phenotypes are also similar: weak activation of eIF3j and TER94 (C60-C61), and doubled frequency of developmental defects (C62) with statistical significance (C63, p<0.05). This convergent evidence from two different circle-loop configurations strongly supports the topology-function relationship.

results.result: The Abd-B TADs (iab-5 through iab-8) exhibit circle-loop topology characterized by interlocking low-density contact (LDC) domains or 'clouds' rather than plumes, consistent with head-to-head boundary pairing.
results.evaluation: The MicroC data in Figure 2B clearly shows the Abd-B TADs lack plumes but display characteristic interlocking LDC domains (C30-C31), with iab-6 showing progressive interactions with immediate and distant neighbors (C32). While the head-to-head pairing orientation (C23) is inferred from prior genetic studies rather than directly demonstrated here, the contact patterns are consistent with circle-loop topology and provide important comparative context for the eve manipulations.

results.result: The CG3294 meta-loop demonstrates head-to-head boundary pairing generating a 2.8 Mb circle-loop, evidenced by upstream-to-upstream and downstream-to-downstream interaction patterns in MicroC.
results.evaluation: The MicroC data in Figure 8A clearly shows the characteristic rectangular boxes of interaction between TADs flanking the paired boundaries (C89). The pattern of upstream-to-upstream and downstream-to-downstream contacts (C90) is diagnostic of head-to-head pairing and circle-loop topology, providing genome-wide validation of the circle-loop signature identified at the eve locus.

results.result: The bin/Mp meta-loop demonstrates head-to-tail boundary pairing generating stem-loops, with brown-green boundaries forming a 2.2 Mb stem-loop and blue-purple boundaries forming a smaller stem-loop bubble.
results.evaluation: The MicroC data in Figure 8B shows a complex meta-loop structure with four boundaries (C91). The interaction patterns are consistent with head-to-tail pairing for both boundary pairs (C92-C93), generating the predicted stem-loop topologies (C94-C95). This provides additional genome-wide evidence for stem-loop structures and validates the MicroC signatures identified at the eve locus.

results.result: Genome-wide analysis suggests that circle-loops are more common than stem-loops in Drosophila (~30 volcano/plume TADs genome-wide), which would exclude cohesin-based loop extrusion as a general mechanism for TAD formation in flies.
results.evaluation: While the survey identifies ~30 volcano/plume TADs genome-wide (C71-C72) and notes that most TADs resemble circle-loops (C73), this analysis is based on MicroC contact patterns that may have ambiguous interpretations (as noted in Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The conclusion that circle-loops exclude loop extrusion (C74) is logical, but the genome-wide frequency estimate requires more systematic validation. The authors appropriately note important caveats about contact pattern interpretation. Direct determination of boundary orientations would be needed to definitively establish the prevalence of each topology.

results.result: Analysis of published mammalian MicroC data suggests that mammalian TADs may also form circle-loops rather than the alternating stem-loop/unanchored loop pattern predicted by the loop extrusion model, with minimal impact from cohesin depletion in some regions.
results.evaluation: The analysis of published mammalian MicroC data (C77, C80-C81) identifies patterns inconsistent with the standard loop extrusion model predictions (C76) and more similar to fly circle-loops (C78-C79). The observation of minimal cohesin impact in the Ppm1g region (C82) is intriguing. However, this analysis is based on reinterpretation of published data rather than new experiments, and the authors appropriately note that resolution limitations and alternative interpretations remain. The implications for mammalian chromosome organization require direct experimental validation.

results.result: The eve TAD structure and neighbor interactions remain unchanged between NC14 embryos (transcriptionally poised) and 12-16 hr embryos (PcG-silenced), suggesting TAD organization is independent of transcriptional state.
results.evaluation: The comparison of MicroC data between developmental stages shows consistent TAD structure despite dramatic changes in transcriptional state (C84, C87), with eve transitioning from poised (C85) to silenced (C86). This provides strong evidence against models where transcriptional state drives TAD formation. However, the analysis is limited to two developmental stages and one locus, so broader generalization requires caution.

results.result: Fly boundaries have insulating activity and form TADs through orientation-dependent pairing, with self-pairing typically head-to-head (possibly for trans-homolog pairing) and heterologous pairing either head-to-head or head-to-tail.
results.evaluation: These claims summarize well-established properties of fly boundaries supported by extensive prior literature (C19-C22, C64-C69). The distinction between PREs (pairing within TADs) and boundaries (defining TAD endpoints) is clearly articulated (C64-C66). The observation that most boundaries pair head-to-head with themselves (C21) and the inference that this may facilitate trans-homolog pairing (C69-C70) are reasonable, though the latter remains somewhat speculative. Fab-7's unusual bidirectional pairing (C67-C68) is appropriately noted as an exception.

results.result: The A/B compartment model proposes that chromatin state determines domain assembly and inter-domain interactions.
results.evaluation: This is an accurate description of the A/B compartment model (C83) and provides necessary context for the Discussion section's critique of this model. The claim itself is descriptive rather than a result of the current study.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that boundary pairing orientation determines TAD topology: head-to-tail pairing (as between nhomie and homie at the eve locus) generates stem-loop TADs, while head-to-head pairing generates circle-loop TADs. This is presented as a general principle supported by prior genetic work and the current experimental manipulations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as a major finding. The editor states the work 'yielded the first demonstration of the existence of stem and circle loops in a genome and confirms a model which had been posited based on extensive prior genetic work.' Reviewer 1 notes 'endogenous Nhomie and Homie boundaries flanking eve pair with head-to-tail directionality to form a chromosomal stem loop' and that inversions 'transformed the stem loop into a circle loop.' No concerns are raised about these core structural claims.

results.result: Wild-type and nhomie forward replacement show the eve TAD as a 'volcano' triangle with plume in MicroC data, with the eve gene sequestered from neighboring TADs (TL and TM), while contacts between the flanking TADs are enhanced, forming the characteristic plume pattern above the volcano triangle.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these MicroC observations as valid descriptions of the stem-loop topology. Reviewer 1 describes the results as 'high-quality' and notes the work 'advances our fundamental understanding of how 3D genome topologies affect enhancer-promoter communication.' The editor calls the evidence 'solid.' While Reviewer 2 raises concerns about quantitative details and methodological rigor, they do not dispute the qualitative MicroC patterns themselves.

results.result: Lambda DNA replacement of nhomie eliminates boundary function, resulting in ill-defined TAD endpoints, ectopic activation of eIF3j by eve enhancers (particularly stripes 1, 2, 3, and 7), and increased frequency of denticle band defects (nearly twofold increase, p<0.01), while eve expression itself appears normal at blastoderm stage.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as demonstrating loss of boundary function. Reviewer 1 states 'Abrogating the Nhomie boundary leads to ectopic activation of genes in the former neighboring TAD by eve embryonic stripe enhancers.' The editor notes the work provides 'insights into how 3D genome topologies affect enhancer–promoter communication.' Reviewer 2 raises concerns about ISH quantification details and requests more methodological information, but does not challenge the core finding of ectopic gene activation.

results.result: Inverting nhomie or replacing it with forward-oriented homie converts the eve TAD from stem-loop to circle-loop topology, reconstituting the TAD but changing contact patterns: the plume is replaced by low-density contact clouds with neighboring TADs, and the eve TAD now interacts with both TL and TM instead of being isolated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this as a key finding. Reviewer 1 states 'Replacing Nhomie by an inverted version or by Homie (which pairs with itself head-to-head) transformed the stem loop into a circle loop' and notes this is 'An important finding.' The editor highlights this as part of the work's contribution to understanding '3D genome topologies.' Reviewer 2 does not challenge these structural observations, though raises broader concerns about interpretation and methodology.

results.result: Circle-loop configurations (nhomie reverse and homie forward) lead to weak ectopic activation of flanking genes (eIF3j and TER94) by eve enhancers in about half of embryos, partial disruption of eve function with increased denticle band defects (nearly twice that of controls, p<0.05), demonstrating compromised regulatory insulation despite intact TAD boundaries.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a significant finding about functional consequences of topology. Reviewer 1 emphasizes 'stem and circle loops differentially impact endogenous gene regulation both within the eve TAD and in the TADs bracketing eve' and notes 'an eve TAD with a circle loop configuration leads to ectopic activation of flanking genes by eve enhancers - indicating compromised regulatory boundary activity despite the presence of an eve TAD with intact left and right boundaries.' Reviewer 2 notes the ISH effects are 'modest' and requests more methodological detail, but does not dispute the findings themselves.

results.result: The Abd-B TADs show distinctive MicroC patterns different from eve: they lack plumes above triangle peaks and instead display rectangular interlocking low-density contact (LDC) domains or 'clouds' connecting neighboring TADs, consistent with head-to-head boundary pairing generating circle-loop topologies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these MicroC observations of Abd-B region. The patterns are presented as supporting evidence for circle-loop topology being more common than stem-loops genome-wide. While Reviewer 2 raises concerns about the interpretation and generalizability of findings, they do not dispute the descriptive MicroC patterns themselves. The editor accepts the evidence as 'solid.'

results.result: Genome-wide survey indicates volcano triangles with plumes (stem-loops) are rare (~30 in non-repetitive regions), while most euchromatic TADs show MicroC profiles resembling circle-loops, suggesting circle-loops may be the predominant topology in the fly genome.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express uncertainty about generalizability. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'the generalizability of TAD formation by directional boundary pairing remains unclear' and notes 'Testing whether boundary pairing is a phenomenon restricted to exceptional loci picked for study, rather than a broader rule of TAD formation, would best be done through the development of untargeted approaches.' The editor notes 'the degree of generalization remains uncertain.' This genome-wide extrapolation is treated as speculative rather than firmly established.

results.result: The authors argue that prevalence of circle-loops in flies excludes cohesin-based loop extrusion as a general TAD formation mechanism, and suggest mammalian genomes may also predominantly use circle-loops rather than the alternating stem-loop/unanchored loop pattern predicted by loop extrusion models.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express significant reservations about these mechanistic interpretations. Reviewer 1 notes 'boundary pairing is one of several mechanisms that may form chromosomal contact domains such as TADs' including 'cohesin-mediated chromosomal loop extrusion' and states 'The functional interplay between these possible TAD-forming mechanisms remains to be further investigated.' Reviewer 2 extensively critiques the lack of consideration of alternative mechanisms, stating the authors provide 'no consideration...to important biophysical properties' and 'no discussion of the biophysical forces that are thought to underly compartmentalization.' These mechanistic claims are treated as insufficiently supported.

results.result: High-resolution RCMC studies in mouse (Goel et al., 2023) show MicroC profiles resembling fly Abd-B circle-loops rather than stem-loops with plumes, and cohesin knockdown has minimal impact on TAD structure in the Ppm1g region, supporting the authors' argument against loop extrusion in mammals.
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not directly challenge these observations from published data, Reviewer 2's critique of the overall mechanistic framework and lack of consideration of compartmentalization models (citing Rowley et al., 2017 showing 'A/B compartmentalization essentially can explain the contact maps observed in Drosophila and other non-vertebrate eukaryotes') suggests skepticism about the authors' interpretation. The comparative analysis is presented but the mechanistic conclusions are questioned.

results.result: The eve TAD structure and interactions with neighbors remain essentially unchanged between NC14 embryos (where eve is transcriptionally poised) and 12-16 hr embryos (where eve is PcG-silenced), indicating TAD organization is independent of transcriptional state.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant concerns about this interpretation, noting 'The contact maps presented in the study represent many cells and distinct cell types' and that 'chromosome conformation is highly variable even within populations of the same cell' with 'structures such as TADs being entirely absent at the single cell level and only appearing upon pseudobulking.' They state 'It is difficult to square these observations with the models of relatively static structures depicted here' and request 'commentary on this point.' This challenges the claim that TAD structure is stable across conditions.

results.result: Meta-loops spanning multiple TADs are observed elsewhere in the genome: a 2.8 Mb circle-loop on chromosome 2L (CG3294 region) formed by head-to-head boundary pairing, and a complex 2.2 Mb structure on chromosome 3L (bin/Mp region) involving four boundaries forming nested stem-loops through head-to-tail pairing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these observations of meta-loop structures. These are presented as additional examples supporting the boundary pairing model. While Reviewer 1 questions generalizability and Reviewer 2 raises methodological concerns, neither disputes these specific MicroC patterns. The examples serve as supporting evidence for the broader claims about boundary pairing mechanisms.

results.result: Background claims about TAD organization, boundary function, orientation-dependence of pairing, PRE function, and the distinction between PREs and boundaries in Drosophila, largely based on prior literature and established knowledge.
results.evaluation: These are presented as established background knowledge supported by extensive citations. Reviewers do not challenge these foundational claims. The editor notes the work 'confirms a model which had been posited based on extensive prior genetic work,' indicating acceptance of the background framework. These claims provide context rather than novel findings.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on stem-loop MicroC observations (C8-C10, C24-C29). Both evaluations find the volcano triangle topology, plume, reduced eve-neighbor contacts, and enhanced TL-TM contacts well-supported. Peer reviewers call evidence 'solid' and 'high-quality,' matching OpenEval's SUPPORTED rating.

Perfect agreement on lambda DNA replacement demonstrating loss of boundary function (C11-C13, C33-C43). Both evaluations accept the MicroC, virtual 4C, HCR-FISH, and cuticle analysis evidence. Peer reviewers request more methodological detail but do not challenge core findings, consistent with OpenEval's SUPPORTED rating.

Strong agreement on foundational claims about TAD formation and boundary pairing (C5-C7, C22-C23). Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as a 'major finding' and note it confirms models from prior genetic work. Both evaluations support these structural claims, though peer review emphasizes this as novel demonstration while OpenEval notes consistency with prior literature.

Strong agreement on nhomie reverse replacement converting stem-loop to circle-loop topology (C14-C16, C44-C50). Both evaluations find MicroC evidence of topology conversion well-supported. Peer reviewers call this 'An important finding,' matching OpenEval's SUPPORTED rating. Shared claims C56-C59 also covered.

Agreement on regulatory disruption in circle-loop configurations (C17, C51-C54). Both evaluations accept HCR-FISH and cuticle defect evidence. Peer reviewers note effects are 'modest' and request methodological detail, but accept findings as significant. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED; peer review also accepts with minor reservations about quantification.

Agreement on homie forward replacement showing circle-loop regulatory phenotypes (C60-C63). Both evaluations accept weak activation of flanking genes and developmental defects. Peer reviewers emphasize this demonstrates 'compromised regulatory boundary activity despite the presence of an eve TAD,' consistent with OpenEval's SUPPORTED rating.

Agreement on Abd-B MicroC observations showing circle-loop characteristics (C30-C32). Both evaluations accept the descriptive MicroC patterns showing LDC domains and progressive interactions. Neither challenges these observations, though OpenEval notes head-to-head pairing (C23) is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

Disagreement on TAD stability across developmental stages (C84-C87). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, finding strong evidence that TAD structure persists despite transcriptional changes. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, noting contact maps represent mixed cell populations and that single-cell studies show TADs may be absent, challenging the static structure interpretation.

Agreement on uncertainty about genome-wide prevalence (C71-C73). Both evaluations express caution about generalizing from ~30 volcano/plume TADs to genome-wide conclusions. OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN noting ambiguous contact pattern interpretations; peer reviewers explicitly state 'generalizability...remains unclear' and call for untargeted approaches.

Agreement on meta-loop MicroC observations (C88-C90). Both evaluations accept the descriptive patterns showing rectangular interaction boxes diagnostic of head-to-head pairing. Neither challenges these specific observations, treating them as supporting evidence for boundary pairing mechanisms.

Agreement on complex meta-loop structures (C91-C95). Both evaluations accept the MicroC patterns showing four-boundary structures with head-to-tail pairing. Neither disputes these observations, which serve as additional genome-wide validation of the boundary pairing model.

Disagreement on mechanistic implications (C74-C75). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting logical inference that circle-loops exclude loop extrusion but requiring validation. Peer reviewers express stronger reservations (UNCERTAIN), emphasizing that 'boundary pairing is one of several mechanisms' and that 'functional interplay...remains to be further investigated.'

Disagreement on loop extrusion model critique (C76-C79). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting reinterpretation of published data requires direct validation. Peer reviewers express significant skepticism (UNCERTAIN), critiquing lack of consideration of alternative mechanisms and stating authors provide 'no consideration...to important biophysical properties.'

Disagreement on mammalian MicroC reanalysis (C80-C82). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting intriguing patterns but requiring experimental validation. Peer reviewers express implicit skepticism (UNCERTAIN) through broader critique of mechanistic framework, citing compartmentalization models as alternative explanations for contact maps.

Agreement on foundational background claims (C19-C22, C64-C70). Both evaluations accept these as established knowledge from prior literature. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED noting well-established properties; peer reviewers accept without challenge, noting work 'confirms a model...posited based on extensive prior genetic work.'

Agreement on basic TAD formation principles (C1-C4). Both evaluations accept these foundational claims about Drosophila TAD formation from prior literature. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as well-established background; peer reviewers accept as established context without challenge.

OpenEval includes descriptive claim about A/B compartment model (C83) as background context for Discussion critique. No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as this is purely descriptive background rather than a study result.

Partial overlap on circle-loop characteristics (C56-C59). OpenEval R6 addresses homie forward replacement showing circle-loop properties; peer R4 addresses both nhomie reverse and homie forward replacements. Both evaluations support the convergent evidence from multiple circle-loop configurations.
